claims.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys can combine low density with high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance through the proposed oxide-film and grain-refinement mechanism.
An inherently stabilized multi-principal-element microstructure facilitates formation of a uniform nanoscale oxide film.
The proposed oxide film is adherent and distributed over the alloy surface.
The proposed oxide film is distributed along grain boundaries.
Mechanical deformation can produce a refined or ultra-nanocrystalline microstructure in a high-entropy alloy.
The alloy's multi-element composition causes slowed diffusion.
A stabilized high-entropy state promotes formation of a protective oxide film during thermal treatment.
The oxide film acts as a barrier that reduces oxygen ingress.
The oxide film acts as a barrier that reduces ingress or uptake of corrosive species.
The oxide layer promotes grain-boundary strengthening.
Grain refinement enhances mechanical strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Inverse Hall-Petch behavior may occur in the nanoscale grain-size regime of a high-entropy alloy.
Controlled oxidation and deformation will increase yield strength relative to a conventionally processed control.
Controlled oxidation and deformation will lower corrosion current density relative to a conventionally processed control.
Controlled oxidation and deformation will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to a conventionally processed control.
The mechanism will cease to hold when substantial deviation from a high-entropy composition causes phase segregation.
Excessively aggressive or high-temperature exposure can destabilize the protective oxide film and eliminate its barrier function.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes increased strength to grain refinement and grain-boundary strengthening, but the mechanism also invokes inverse Hall-Petch behavior in the nanoscale regime. Inverse Hall-Petch behavior generally denotes loss of strength with further grain refinement, so it does not coherently support the unqualified prediction of increased yield strength.
